name: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome
aliases: jumper's knee of the growing patella

reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella rather than a true osteonecrosis
Affected site is the lower pole of the patella at the origin of the proximal patellar tendon
Typically affects active children and young adolescents, roughly ten to fourteen years of age
Presents with anterior knee pain and tenderness localised to the inferior patellar pole, aggravated by running, jumping and stair climbing
The radiographic hallmark is fragmentation or calcification at the inferior pole of the patella
It is essentially the patellar counterpart of Osgood-Schlatter disease, occurring at the opposite (proximal) end of the extensor mechanism
Pain is reproduced by resisted knee extension and by palpation of the distal patellar pole
Management is conservative with activity modification, extensor mechanism stretching and strengthening, and physiotherapy as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome is a traction apophysitis affecting the inferior pole of the patella, where the proximal fibres of the patellar tendon attach to the still-developing lower patellar margin. Repetitive, forceful contraction of the quadriceps during jumping and running transmits tension through the patellar tendon to this immature bone-tendon junction. The repeated microtrauma produces small avulsive injuries, inflammation and reactive calcification or fragmentation at the inferior patellar pole. It is analogous to Osgood-Schlatter disease but occurs at the proximal rather than the distal attachment of the patellar tendon, and it typically resolves as the patella matures and the traction stresses of rapid growth subside.
additionalDifferentials: Osgood-Schlatter disease at the tibial tubercle
Patellar sleeve or inferior pole avulsion fracture
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination localising tenderness to the inferior patellar pole
Lateral knee radiographs showing fragmentation or calcification at the lower patellar pole
Ultrasound to assess the proximal patellar tendon and inferior pole
Magnetic resonance imaging in atypical or persistent cases
Assessment of quadriceps and hamstring flexibility and lower limb alignment
Comparison with the contralateral knee to distinguish from a bipartite patella
redFlags: Acute severe pain with an extensor lag suggesting a patellar sleeve or avulsion fracture
Rest pain, night pain or systemic features raising concern for infection or malignancy
A joint effusion or mechanical locking pointing to intra-articular pathology
Failure to improve with conservative measures prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is favourable; symptoms are self-limiting and typically resolve as the patella matures and traction loads decrease, with activity modification and rehabilitation controlling pain and no significant long-term sequelae.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with Osgood-Schlatter disease at the opposite end of the extensor mechanism
Mistaking a bipartite patella or an avulsion fracture for the apophysitis
Overlooking a patellar sleeve fracture in a child with acute severe anterior knee pain
Failing to correct extensor mechanism tightness that perpetuates the traction injury
management: Activity modification with relative rest from jumping and running to offload the inferior patellar pole, the mainstay given the self-limiting course
Simple analgesia or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and local ice for pain control
Physiotherapy with quadriceps and hamstring stretching and progressive strengthening, correcting inflexibility of the extensor mechanism
Patellar tendon strap or taping and a graded return-to-sport programme
Reassurance that symptoms resolve as the patella matures and traction loads decline
Reassessment with imaging in atypical or persistent cases to exclude other anterior knee pathology
